title: Why mPharma Stopped Digitising Prescriptions and Took On the Stock
dek: mPharma began in 2013 by trying to put prescriptions online; by 2017 Gregory Rockson had it managing pharmacies' stock, because the drugs were not on the shelves.

story.event: Moving from a digital prescription tool to managing independent pharmacies' drug inventory
story.summary: mPharma, founded in Accra in 2013 by Gregory Rockson, Daniel Shoukimas and James Finucane, began with a digital prescription tool meant to show doctors and patients where drugs were in stock, piloted at a hospital in Lusaka. By 2017 it had changed course to managing small pharmacies' inventory: forecasting demand, buying in bulk, financing stock and carrying the risk of over- or under-stocking, which Rockson said answered the stockouts caused by Africa's order-driven supply chain.
paragraphs: In November 2014 Gregory Rockson, chief executive of mPharma, began a post on the company blog with a death. About a year earlier, it said, a woman in a Ghanaian hospital had died while doctors waited for drugs and supplies the hospital did not have. Her son spent two hours looking for a pharmacy that had them, and came back to find she had died.

Rockson's diagnosis then was mostly about information. Drugs expired in one place while patients went without in another, and more than 99% of prescriptions in Africa, he wrote, were still written by hand. mPharma, founded in 2013 with Daniel Shoukimas and James Finucane, set out to replace the prescription pad with a digital tool linked to stock information. From August 2013 it ran a pilot with Zambia's health ministry at Levy Mwanawasa General Hospital in Lusaka, which showed, for one, that a free substitute for cephalexin was going undispensed. He was candid about the obstacles: most health facilities lacked basic internet.

By early 2017, according to a later analysis on a Harvard Business School site, the prescription network had been set aside. It had captured what doctors wrote but little about what pharmacies stocked, sold or charged. mPharma instead took over the stock of small independent pharmacies: forecasting demand, buying on their combined behalf and financing the inventory, and, as UN Dispatch put it in 2019, carrying the financial risk when drugs were over- or under-stocked. Rockson now described the problem as one of ordering: distributors waited for purchase orders, so "both parties are unable to forecast demand which leads to frequent stockouts."

In November 2017 mPharma raised a $6.6 million Series A. It then served more than 70 outlets in four countries, mostly private hospital pharmacies, and said it had cut some patients' drug costs by up to 30%. By 2019 it counted 243 pharmacies and clinics in its network, and that year it bought 85% of Haltons, Kenya's second-largest pharmacy chain. The road was not smooth: in September 2023 it cut about 150 staff, which Rockson put down to the steep fall of the Nigerian naira. In 2025 he handed the chief executive's role to Kwesi Arhin and became chairman.

quote.text: The thoughtless man, even if he can recite a large portion (of the law), but is not a doer of it, has no share in the priesthood, but is like a cowherd counting the cows of others.
quote.source_title: Dhammapada, a Collection of Verses, tr. F. Max Müller, Project Gutenberg eBook #2017
quote.connection: The verse is hard on knowledge that never becomes action. mPharma's first tool counted other people's prescriptions and stock; by 2017 it held the stock itself. Yet it still builds datasets and sells market intelligence, and the line between counting a herd and tending it is thinner than the verse allows.

reflection: Rockson's first answer was a sensible one, and the pilot taught real things. It still was not where the medicine was getting stuck. His later explanation was about orders and shelves, not prescriptions, and the company changed what it did to match.

You will have a first answer to most problems, and it will often be partly right. When something keeps failing anyway, it can help to stand where the failure actually happens, at the shelf, the bench or the front desk, and watch for a while before deciding what to fix next.
invitation: Pick one problem that keeps coming back in your week. Before trying another fix, spend twenty minutes where it actually happens and write down one thing you had not expected to see.

cross_checks.claim: mPharma was founded in 2013 by Rockson, Shoukimas and Finucane
mPharma's first product was a digital prescription tool linked to drug stock information
By 2017 mPharma was managing independent pharmacies' inventory, forecasting demand and financing stock
mPharma raised a $6.6 million Series A in November 2017

research_notes: Slate framing adjusted: mPharma did not begin by managing pharmacy inventory. Rockson's own November 2014 post describes a digital prescription tool piloted in Zambia from August 2013, and the HBS Digital Initiative piece dates the move to vendor-managed inventory to early 2017; so the arc is change-of-direction and the date 2017, and the story's country is Ghana, where the company is based (the pilot was in Zambia). TechCrunch's boilerplate says mPharma was founded 'to manage prescription drug inventory'; the contemporary 2014 post is preferred. Founding year: 2013 (TechCrunch, HBS piece, the 2014 post's August 2013 pilot) versus 2014 (Skoll profile, Launch Base Africa) and 'three-year-old' in November 2017 (Quartz via Graphic); 2013 used. Westminster College says Rockson (class of 2012) co-founded mPharma while still a student; not used. The HBS piece is an MBA student's analysis, not a faculty case; it is attributed as 'a later analysis on a Harvard Business School site'. It also says mPharma lost Pfizer, its major customer, in 2016; no second source was found, so that is left out. Network size is counted differently over time: more than 70 outlets (2017, Quartz), 243 pharmacies and clinics (Westminster, 2019), 300 partner pharmacies (TechCrunch, March 2021) and 200 community pharmacies (TechCrunch, January 2022); the story gives only the 2017 and 2019 figures with their dates. Savings: up to 30% in some cases (Quartz, 2017) vs 30-60% (Westminster, 2019); the conservative 2017 claim is used and attributed to the company. The 2023 layoffs and 2025 leadership change rest on Launch Base Africa alone and are stated with Rockson's own stated reason only. The Rockson quotation is from Quartz's 2017 report as republished by Graphic Online (qz.com blocks automated requests). The 2014 blog post is cited from the Internet Archive because mpharma.com did not load; the post names its author only as the CEO with a contact address, which, with its 'From our CEO' category, identifies Rockson. The Internet Archive copy (capture of 16 July 2019) was briefly unreachable during checking and then loaded again; a later mPharma Medium post ('One year into e-prescriptions at mPharma') confirms the e-prescription phase but blocks automated requests and was not read, so it is not cited.
